title: A Shoemaker Bought a Uniform and Arrested a Mayor #shorts

authoring.run: scheduled short run, 20 Nov 2026; first slate idea (case 043)

description:
Case 043. In October 1906 a man in a Prussian captain's uniform stopped ten passing soldiers, ordered them to follow him, and led them to the town hall of Köpenick, near Berlin. There he had the mayor and the treasurer arrested, had over 4,000 marks handed over from the town treasury, walked out with the money and vanished. The soldiers had obeyed him without question; so had everyone else. There was no captain. He was Wilhelm Voigt, an out-of-work shoemaker with a prison record, and the uniform was second-hand, from a shop. He was caught ten days later and sentenced to four years in prison. After less than two, Kaiser Wilhelm II pardoned him (the Kaiser is reported to have been amused by the affair), and Voigt went on tour, playing the Captain of Köpenick on stage. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The rooms, streets, uniforms and everyone in them are generic low-poly shapes with no real insignia, crests or logos, and nobody's likeness is attempted. Staging details such as the look of the office, the treasury, the shop, the alley, the cell, the palace study and the theatre, and where people stood, are illustrative. Narrated with a synthetic voice (Kokoro).

Sources: Wikipedia, 'Wilhelm Voigt'; Museum of Hoaxes, 'The Captain of Köpenick'; HistoryNet, 'Captain of Köpenick' (Military History, October 2006).

source_notes: Read for this run on 20 Nov 2026 through a fetch tool, three pages loaded: Wikipedia 'Wilhelm Voigt' (the article carries a 'needs additional citations' tag); Museum of Hoaxes, 'The Captain of Köpenick' (Alex Boese); HistoryNet, 'Captain of Köpenick' (Verner Markussen, Military History, October 2006). The two links on the slate (Wikipedia 'Captain of Köpenick' and History.com) could not be opened in this run: the fetch tool asked for a permission nobody was there to give, so they were not used. Every narrated fact and label is on at least two of the three pages read. October 1906: all three (16 October: Wikipedia and Museum of Hoaxes). A shoemaker: all three; out of work: Museum of Hoaxes ('out-of-work'), HistoryNet (could not get work without papers). A prison record: Wikipedia (sentences adding up to 25 years, released February 1906) and HistoryNet ('short stints of prison'); the two disagree on how much, so the narration says only 'a prison record'. A second-hand captain's uniform from a shop: all three (Wikipedia: parts from different shops). Ten soldiers: Wikipedia (four grenadiers stopped near a barracks, a sergeant sent away, six more from a shooting range) and HistoryNet (a platoon of ten that passed and saluted); Museum of Hoaxes says a company 'marching past'. The narration says 'ten men who happened to be passing, ordered to follow him'; the animation shows them as one group of ten in a street, which simplifies Wikipedia's two groups. Köpenick town hall, near Berlin; the mayor and the treasurer arrested: all three (on a pretext of corruption or embezzlement; the pretext is not narrated). Over 4,000 marks from the town treasury: Wikipedia (4,002 marks 37 pfennigs) and HistoryNet ('more than 4,000'); Museum of Hoaxes says 4,000. Handed over on his order: HistoryNet; Wikipedia says he took it against a receipt. He left with the money and disappeared: all three. Caught ten days later: Wikipedia (26 October) and HistoryNet; Museum of Hoaxes says nine days; the label follows the two that agree with the dates. Sentenced to four years: all three. Pardoned by the Kaiser after less than two years: Museum of Hoaxes ('less than two years') and Wikipedia (pardoned 16 August 1908, 20 months served); HistoryNet says only 'soon granted a free pardon'. The Kaiser's amusement is reported, not established: Wikipedia ('claims that even the Kaiser was amused'), HistoryNet ('is reported to have laughed out loud'); the narration says 'reportedly amused' and no words are put in his mouth. Went on tour playing the captain on stage: Museum of Hoaxes (re-enacting his stunt on the stage), Wikipedia (variety shows, small theatres, a play about his exploit), HistoryNet (toured with circuses as the Captain of Köpenick). Not used because only one page read gives them: the train ride to Köpenick, the receipt signed with his old prison warden's name, the carriages to Berlin, the order to stand guard for half an hour, the passport motive, the former cellmate's tip, the statue. Staging liberties, all illustrative: the hook shows bayonets levelled at the mayor in his office and the mayor putting his hands up (the sources say he was arrested by the soldiers, not how); the treasury, safe and cash box; the captain inspecting a line of soldiers and the soldiers left standing at the town hall; the removal of the cap in an alley; the cobbler's room; the arrest by two policemen in an alley; the palace study, the newspaper and the stamp; the theatre, its audience and the flowers; Rook is fictional. The man shown pardoning him is a generic figure with an upturned moustache, not a likeness.

experiments.E1_E2: spine v2: Rook is already in the office in shot 5, sitting on the mayor's desk, and doubts it in one line of 1.3 s ('Arrested for what, exactly?') with the arrest still in frame; no cutaway to his office. The story runs forward from the arrest to the money and the walk-out, then turns once at the re-hook (who the captain really was and how he did it) and goes forward again to the arrest, the pardon and the stage. Place, date and names are labels (KÖPENICK, NEAR BERLIN; OCTOBER 1906; WILHELM VOIGT, SHOEMAKER).
experiments.E3: The batch brief's Shorts are all made, so this Short is outside it. It opens on a person close-up: the mayor at his desk, eyes wide, with bayonets arriving 0.1 s in.
experiments.E8: tail 0.4 s; the last line ('Because near Berlin, in nineteen oh six,') runs into the first ('a captain marches ten soldiers into a town hall...'); the last shot closes in on the mayor at his desk and ends on the opening shot's first frame (checked: first and last frames of the rehearsal side by side).

sound_plan.first_frame: Near-silence under the hook title, then a 'hit' at 0.1 s as the bayonets come in (the gate needs an impact in the first second; here it is the story's own sound), a clunk and a gasp.
sound_plan.music: The engine's score follows the segment moods: hook, tense for Rook's line, action for the cash, tense for the obedience, calm for the walk-out, tense for the re-hook, wonder for the shop and the street, action for the arrest, calm for the pardon (with the hush), triumph for the stage, end.
sound_plan.effects: One to five cues a shot, each tied to something visible: boot stamps (clunk) for marching and halting, a shout for the order, ticks for notes and coins, a hit when the bayonet drops in front of Rook, hammer hits at the cobbler's bench, a gasp for Rook's shock, a creak for the cell door, a clunk for the stamp, caws for Rook's laugh.
sound_plan.hush: Shot 25 (the cell door opens and the old man walks out): the music drops out under 'reportedly amused, pardons him.'
sound_plan.voice: Narration is ducked over the bed by the engine; measured in the local rehearsal, not listened to.

quality_gate.method: One run, five review rounds. Round 1: low-res contact sheet of all 30 shots: the floor-level camera sat inside the desk, the captain hid the treasurer, the cap's visor pointed up, the portal's pediment was upside down, the theatre's seat backs were in front of the sitters, the cap and the boot covered faces, the release and the arrest were too dark; all fixed. Round 2: sheet again: the cash shot was mostly empty table, the dummy was out of frame in the shop, the Kaiser was hidden behind his paper and desk, the open cell door hid the old man, Rook was hidden behind the bowing captain; all fixed. Round 3: every shot previewed at k=0.2 and 0.8: the captain walked down the line with his back to us (turned round), rifles crossed his face in the doorway (rifles on shoulders), the opening of the loop shot started inside the door wall, the cell release was reframed. Round 4: full rehearsal (12 fps, 360x640): local gate PASS: 30 shots, mean 1.50 s, longest 2.70 s, Rook acting in 12 of 30 shots (40%), -14.6 LUFS, peak -1.3 dBFS, voice 18.0 dB over the bed, closest match to any earlier episode 0.61 (shot 7 against r023-herfkens; the limit is 0.93). Reviewed as a 4 fps sheet of the whole video. Round 5: the first place label overlapped the hook title (moved one shot later) and the captain was too small in the walk-out (camera moved in, that shot re-rendered); recomposited, local gate PASS again with the same figures; first and last frames compared side by side for the loop. Duration 44.9 s. The cloud render runs the real gate at 720x1280 and 60 fps.
quality_gate.not_met: Loudness range measured 2.4 LU against the checklist's 4 LU (the narration alone measures 1.7 LU and runs almost wall to wall, so this comes from the engine's mix and the format, not from this episode; earlier approved episodes record the same). The soundtrack was measured, not listened to. One full local rehearsal instead of a watch-through at full resolution.

review.weakest: Humans are block figures with simple faces. In the walk-out the captain is small and the caption sits over him for a moment. The interiors have no ceilings, so the top of some frames is black. In the cash shot the glove's arm reads as a plain blue bar and the treasurer's hand is unclear. The man who pardons him is small behind his desk for the first half-second while the newspaper is up. Rook is cut by the left edge for part of his line on the desk. Narration and sound were measured, not heard.
